summary.text: Acceleration measures how rapidly and in what direction an object changes its velocity.
Applying a net force to an object produces acceleration aligned with that force, proportional to the force's magnitude and inversely proportional to mass.
Acceleration includes both changes in speed and changes in direction, such as moving along a circular path at constant speed.

facts.label: Relativistic limit
facts.value: Relativistic effects grow as speeds near light speed

facts.label: Uniform acceleration example
facts.value: An object in free fall in a uniform gravitational field

items.prompt: If a car travels along a straight road while steadily picking up speed, what form of acceleration is taking place?

options.label: Linear or tangential acceleration
Radial acceleration
Deceleration or retardation
Centripetal acceleration

items.explain: When an object speeds up along a straight line without changing direction, the acceleration occurs in the direction of its motion, which is called linear or tangential acceleration.

items.prompt: A satellite orbits Earth in a circle at a steady speed. Why is it still considered to be accelerating?

options.label: Its mass decreases while orbiting.
Its direction of travel is constantly changing.
Its speed increases during each orbit.
It experiences a retro-rocket force.

items.explain: Acceleration includes changes in direction as well as speed; turning along a circular path causes centripetal acceleration even if speed stays constant.

items.prompt: How does doubling the total force on an object change its acceleration if the mass stays the same?

options.label: The acceleration is reduced by half.
The acceleration remains completely unchanged.
The acceleration doubles in magnitude.
The acceleration quadruples in magnitude.

items.explain: According to Newton's second law, net acceleration is directly proportional to the magnitude of the net force acting on the mass.

items.prompt: A stone falls near Earth's surface with no air resistance. What alone sets how fast its velocity changes?

options.label: The size and weight of the stone
The height it was released from
How hard it was pushed at the start
The strength of the gravitational field

items.explain: With no resistance to motion, a falling body's acceleration depends only on the gravitational field strength g.

items.prompt: Why is average acceleration considered the most fundamental way to measure acceleration?

options.label: It can be measured directly without appealing to empirical laws.
It is the only measurement that has a direction vector.
It eliminates the need to record elapsed time.
It remains constant regardless of applied net force.

items.explain: Average acceleration requires only the change in velocity and change in time, making it the only true acceleration measurable without relying on empirical physics laws.

items.prompt: What happens to the acceleration vector when a driver steps on the brakes to slow down a moving car?

options.label: The acceleration turns perpendicular to the path.
The acceleration acts opposite to the direction of velocity.
The acceleration vector drops immediately to zero.
The acceleration converts entirely into radial acceleration.

items.explain: Slowing down, often called deceleration, is acceleration directed opposite to the object's velocity vector.

paragraphs.heading: What acceleration is
paragraphs.text: Acceleration measures how fast an object's velocity is changing, and in which direction. Like velocity, it has both a size and a direction, which makes it a vector quantity. Its SI unit is the metre per second squared, m/s², also read as metres per second per second. The name fits: each second, the velocity in metres per second changes by the value of the acceleration.

paragraphs.heading: Speeding up, slowing down, turning
paragraphs.text: Picture a car pulling away from a standstill and gaining speed on a straight road: it is accelerating in the direction it travels. If the car turns, there is an acceleration toward the new direction. If it slows down, the acceleration points against its velocity, which is called deceleration or retardation. Physics treats speeding up and slowing down the same way, since both are changes in velocity. Passengers feel each one, pushed back into their seats, thrown forward when braking, or, on a bend, what is called centrifugal force.

paragraphs.heading: The parts of an acceleration
paragraphs.text: Tangential acceleration is the part that points along the direction of motion. When the direction of the velocity stays the same, this is called linear acceleration. Radial or normal acceleration is the part that changes the direction of the velocity; in circular motion it is called centripetal, meaning it points toward the centre. So a satellite circling the Earth is accelerating even if its speed never changes, because its direction keeps changing.

paragraphs.heading: Force and mass
paragraphs.text: In Newtonian mechanics, acceleration comes from the forces acting on a mass, and the net acceleration results from the net force. By Newton's second law, the size of the acceleration grows in proportion to the net force and shrinks as the mass gets larger, and it points the same way as the net force. For a body of constant mass this is written 𝐅 = m𝐚, so 𝐚 = 𝐅/m. The second law is normally used in an inertial reference frame.

paragraphs.heading: Average, instant and uniform
paragraphs.text: Strictly, average acceleration is the only kind that can be measured directly without leaning on an empirical law. Instantaneous acceleration is what the average becomes as the time interval shrinks toward zero. Uniform acceleration means the velocity changes by the same amount in every equal stretch of time. The classic case is free fall in a uniform gravitational field, where, with no resistance, the acceleration depends only on the field strength g. Such motion can be split into two parts at right angles: one at constant velocity, the other following the falling motion just described. Galileo showed that together they give a parabola, the path of a projectile in a vacuum near Earth's surface.

paragraphs.heading: Feeling it from the inside
paragraphs.text: Inside a frame that is itself accelerating, Newton's laws still work if you add a fictitious force, F = −ma, pointing opposite to the frame's acceleration. That is why someone riding an elevator feels heavier or lighter while it speeds up or slows down. An instrument called an accelerometer measures proper acceleration, which is acceleration compared with free fall. In general relativity, gravity and inertial acceleration may be impossible to tell apart locally.
